segment.text: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。

segment.text: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。

cast.first_person: 俺 (only in plural 俺たち, p25) — rough, intimate masculine first person; what it says is youth, working-class plainness, and unguarded solidarity with his wife, not authority

default narrator reference throughout; never named, never 旦那 or honorific — keep as man / young father
third-person pronoun for him (p8, p9); narrator also uses 彼女 for both mother and baby, so 彼 is the only pronoun that unambiguously marks him — do not collapse into he/him without checking antecedent
used once in p18 when mother glances at 夫と子供; marks him as seen through her eyes on return from vision
wife never names or titles him in dialogue; husband addresses wife only with bare questions どうして黙ってるの / なぜ黙ってるの — intimacy is in the absence of terms

hard_spots.why_hard: Potato is hard as if frozen (凍ったかのやうに固く), gritty/crunchy (ざくざく), extremely unpleasant, flavourless, cold, and pointedly かかはりのない — unconnected to her. No cause (undercooked, raw) is given. English must stay flat sensation-report, not explain cooking failure or gloss as symbol; that flatness is the trigger that gives her a quiet, lonely, far-off heart.

Long, syntactically loose sentences repeat ながい, 絶えることなく, 静かに安らかに, 微笑, 懐しみと許し, 安らかさ. Figures, place and time unnamed; p17 widens from her mind to general truth (世の中の總ての事、人生は過去るであらう…) and returns to her sigh in p18. Do not paragraph-break into heaven, caption as old age/death, or fuse the seam with 'she realised'. Keep repetition dull and duration felt.

Child fixed once as 女の子 then twice called 坊や by mother. English must decide house-wide (keep Bōya with note vs neutral baby) and not silently correct to boy or girl-name; each option changes period texture. Do not let pronoun choice later drift the child male.

卓《テーブル》, 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほほゑみ》 ruby; 茶碗, 土瓶, アルミ鍋, 藍色の深い鍋 with beef/onion/carrot/potato. Do not import a dish-name (e.g. nikujaga/stew) or explain aluminium; keep plain objects. Ruby shows reading help for contemporary readers, not emphasis — no italics needed in English for these.

Exchange is short, repeated, almost empty: どうして黙ってるの / なぜ黙ってるの, さうだなァ, 本当にね, まだ三年しか経たないんですものね. Husband plain-masculine 俺たち…なァ; wife polite のね/ませうね. Do not turn into heart-to-heart with beats of realisation, do not warm husband into obtuseness or tenderness, do not add psychology (she resolved/consoled herself). Emptiness is the intimacy.

小さな乳首をだして乳をのませ初めた; child with cheek to breast, eyes closed; clearing up, early rising tomorrow; whispered standing-still 嵐だな answering opening 嵐だ. Must stay plain, bodily, quiet — not cosy family tableau, not symbolic closure. Keep both storm sentences bare and alike.

motifs.english: Keep one small family: smile / smile / laughing. Do not vary to grin, chuckle, beam. Opening laughter is overflowing, helpless, forgetful exhaustion; vision smiling is motionless. Same word, changed state.
motifs.why: Network binds parents' helpless laughter at table to the still smiling of the vision figures. Varying it for elegance would dissolve the spell and hide that the same act has stilled.

motifs.english: Keep weariness / tiredness throughout; drowsy, sunken, deep. Do not upgrade to exhaustion-as-theme or downgrade to sleepiness.
source_forms: 打沈んだやうな深い疲れ
motifs.why: Establishes the fatigue double: faces still unwrinkled and young yet already carrying deep tiredness. The whole story tests p4's promise that night's rest will wash the day away.

motifs.english: Keep quiet / quietly / stillness as the same word. Do not vary to calm, gentle, silent for variety.
motifs.why: Moves from interior detachment (静かな淋しい遠くはなれた心) to vision stillness (物静か, 静かに安らかに) to returned house quiet (静まりかへった). One word tracks absorption and return.

motifs.english: Keep far / far-off / distant. Spatial word doing temporal work.
motifs.why: The mother's distance is rendered as space: staring far off, remembering with a far heart, seeing a far picture. Must recur, not be paraphrased as absent-minded or wistful.

motifs.english: Keep the exact paired phrase every time: nostalgia/longing and forgiveness. Do not alternate nostalgia/forgiveness with yearning/pardon, and do not shorten to one half.

motifs.why: The crux phrase. Everything will only on the day after passing turn into this pair. Identical repetition is the doctrine; synonyms rewrite it.

motifs.english: Keep peace / restfulness / rest. Same root for feeling and for night-like rest at end. Do not render as comfort, relief, serenity in rotation.
motifs.why: Tests p4: night's 安らかさ promised cheaply at start returns as deep peace of vision and as eternal night-like rest. Varying the English hides the test.

motifs.english: Keep long as long — dull, unvaried. Long story, long life, long suffering, endlessly continuing.
motifs.why: Deliberately monotonous duration-word. Finding synonyms (lengthy, protracted, eternal) would ennoble what the author keeps flat to make duration felt.

motifs.english: Keep like a dream and like a phantom picture as stated similes; do not harden into dream / hallucination nouns.
motifs.motif: like a dream, like a phantom
motifs.why: Marks the mother's defamiliarisation without marking it as dream, heaven or prophecy. Hardening it explains what text leaves open.

motifs.english: Keep storm and sound of rain-wind bare and alike in p1 and p38; keep the two not-hearings (p8) and hearings (p19). Barometer of absorption and return.
source_forms: 雨風の音を耳にしない
嵐の音を静かに耳にした
motifs.why: Frame: opens on storm, closes on storm. Forgetting it (laughter/noise) then hearing it again (quiet) measures her displacement. Must not be varied to tempest/gale or psychologised.

motifs.english: Keep three / three people / three years with numerals audible. Do not smooth away the echo, and do not state identity.
motifs.why: Three at table, three figures, barely three years — echo the reader will want to resolve into 'themselves grown old'. Keep the numbers identical so the echo sounds, without captioning it.

narration.english_tense: Past as default for narrative and interior report; keep gnomic present only where Japanese widens to general truth, chiefly p17 (life passes / everything turns…). Do not backshift vision into had-seen pluperfect explanation and do not present-tense the table bustle for vividness.
narration.frame: Single-evening interior, storm-enclosed: storm announced (p1) → crowded supper and laughter (p2–p9) → private detachment inside one mouthful (p10–p15) → vision and gloss (p16–p17) → sigh and return glance (p18) → noticed silence and unconfessed exchange about three years (p19–p35) → nursing, clearing, sleep, whispered storm (p36–p38). Evening unchanged; only her distance moved.
narration.narrator: Heterodiegetic third person, lyrical Taishō literary voice in historical kana; starts as even observer of the tableau, slides from p10 into mother's free-indirect interior without signals, widens toward aphorism in p17, then withdraws to plain exterior report. Never judges, never explains, never names.
narration.tense_habits: Historical-kana literary mix: past progressive ていた for tableau and ongoing action, stative ている / てゐる for states that persist into present, sudden present する for storm and gnomic statements, ところ・やうだ hedges for seeing-as. Viewpoint melts with tense from p10: longer looser sentences, subject-dropping, repetition replacing event.
timeline: One night only, during a storm: supper in a small room under a dark electric light
Married three years past (p14, p22, p25, p27); baby pre-walking, ~1 year; two years of hardship already gone, walking and work still ahead (p28, p34–p36)
Vision-time is unbounded: endless story, life after passing, eternal night-like rest (p16–p17) — no date, no place, deliberately unlocated

body.say: A single-evening story that stands or falls on keeping the mother's vision still, repetitive and unexplained while the housework continues around it; hold every repeated word, both clocks (still young / already old, barely three years / endless), and the storm frame without warming, explaining or resolving them.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Minimal. No in-prose glosses for period food, aluminium pot, electric light, breastfeeding, or Bōya. Note only what sentence cannot give: e.g. one note on 坊や for a girl if Bōya is kept, one note on historical kana/ruby if edition policy needs it. Must pass the keikaku-means-plan test.
style_sheet.author_voice: Lyrical but not ornate; crowded, physical, repetitive at table (fat hands, banging, bolting rice), then lengthening and incantatory in vision. Keep paratactic plainness and deliberate dull repetition; resist ennoblement, clarification, and added psychology (she realised/resolved/consoled herself). Let ordinary resolutions — work, clear up, sleep, rise early — stay ordinary.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No personal names in text; keep role-terms in English lower case (young father, mother, baby) and never invent names. Keep 先生-style retention out — not applicable. For 坊や see keep_in_japanese: do not silently normalise to baby-boy or pet name without house decision and note.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: 坊や as Bōya (italicised, capital B) if house accepts untranslated address — because the clash girl-called-Bōya is textual data; otherwise neutral baby with a margin note recording the loss. No other Japanese retention needed; do not import dish-names. Macrons for romanisation where used (Bōya).
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 『』 for direct speech and ひとりごと思考独言; render in English double quotes with minimal tags, preserving unattributed turns and silences (p19, p21). Keep interior độc thoại (とふと口の中に独言…) distinct from spoken lines without adding 'she thought'.
style_sheet.register: Narrator: plain literary English, slightly period but not archaic; avoid modern colloquial bounce. Dialogue: husband plain rough-masculine, wife polite feminine-desu/masu; keep the gap audible without caricature or dialect.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Source ruby (卓《テーブル》, 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほほゑみ》, 茫然《ぼんやり》, 希《のぞみ》) is period reading-aid, not emphasis — do not carry into English as italics or parentheses. Use italics only for kept Japanese (Bōya) and, sparingly, for the babble うまうま if needed.

head.reason: They name the same crux in different words: a present left materially and psychologically unredeemed, made bearable only from an unmarked, undecidable retrospect in which it is already past. Option 1's second point about the two time-registers and the storm's circular return is Option 0's structural evidence made explicit — the frame that shows only her distance has moved — not a different crux, and Option 1 gives that sameness in more checkable English directives (unmarked slide, unresolved conjectures, repeated words, flat domestic exchanges). Option 0 got the husband-warning right — neither antagonist nor rescuer — but the text that goes forward is Option 1 as written.
head.say:
Pick: Option 1. They name the same crux — consolation only in retrospect, the present untouched — and Option 1's time-and-storm point is Option 0's frame made explicit, not a second crux.

House log: Ruled the two crux statements the same and adopted the crux check's wording as written.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the slide unmarked and the vision unresolved: do not name it heaven, death, old age, or a flash-forward, do not convert its だらう / ようだ conjectures into certainty, and do not explain the potato as a symbol. Let the same repeated words — quiet, rest/peace, nostalgia/dearness, forgiveness, far, dream — accumulate in long, looping sentences rather than varying or compressing them for elegance.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on the mother's unmarked drift from the bad potato into a distant, end-of-life perspective in which the whole of life is already past and transfigured into nostalgia and forgiveness — while it remains undecidable whether that picture is death, extreme old age, or pure reverie.
crux.why: The turn is triggered by nothing grander than a grittily cold, tasteless potato (p11–p12), then the narration slips without signal from supper into p16's dim tableau of three motionless figures telling an endless story containing all good, evil, sorrow and joy, and p17's assertion that only on the day life has passed will everything change into 懐しみと許し. The shock of the piece is that this total retrospect is applied to a marriage of barely three years (p13–p14): she feels wholly aged, yet objectively almost nothing has elapsed.

crux.for_the_english: Preserve the durational loop and the circular weather: keep the repetitions and tense drift of the reverie, keep the short domestic exchanges flat and unadorned against it, and let the final 『嵐だな』 land as a return of the opening line rather than new information. Do not tidy the chronology (already three years / only three years / two years past) into a consistent summary.
crux.point: Time is experienced in two incompatible registers at once — one noisy evening and three exhausting years that feel like a lifetime, consoled only by projecting the redemptive 'that day' into an indefinite future and then immediately re-entering work and tomorrow.
crux.why: The storm opens the story (p1), is forgotten in the child's racket (p8), is first heard again inside the reverie itself (p19), and returns as the closing whisper (p38). Between those brackets the dialogue keeps recalculating the same span — 'only three years', 'already two years gone', 'a little longer' (p22–p35) — and the consolation of p20 resolves into nothing more visionary than nursing the child, clearing the table, and rising early tomorrow (p35–p36).

second.say: The crux (one or two items), each with its reason and what follows for the English; a line on how confident you are and what would change your mind. Keep it under a page.
second.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence from Shizu's other writing or contemporary context that the p16 picture is a specific, recognisable doctrine or set-piece (e.g. a Buddhist or Christian afterlife scene) with a fixed referent — that would license naming what I would otherwise leave indeterminate.

body.why: The 38-paragraph story totals only about 3,400 characters with no chapters or scene breaks, so it forms a single arc best held whole in one reading.

crux.for_the_english: So: do not make the vision an explanation, a heaven, or a decision. Keep it still, repetitive, and unresolved, and let the return to work, breastfeeding, clearing up, and tomorrow be as plain as it is. Do not add psychology — 'she realised', 'she consoled herself', 'she resolved' — that the narration withholds, and do not warm the husband into obtuseness or tenderness to give the scene an antagonist or a rescuer.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on the mother's vision and on what is *not* done with it. A badly cooked potato — hard, gritty, tasteless in her mouth — does not prompt complaint, memory in the ordinary sense, or rebellion. It detaches her. Three years of married poverty suddenly feel like a whole lifetime already lived, she feels already old, and she sees, as in a dim picture, three quiet figures with heads together endlessly telling one another a story that contains all good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, trouble and joy, while nobody moves and everybody smiles, wrapped in nostalgia and forgiveness and a deep peace. The thought that follows is the crux: life passes, and only on the day after it has passed does everything turn to nostalgia and forgiveness, before an eternal, night-like rest. Consolation here is entirely retrospective and posthumous in feeling — the present is not redeemed, improved, or even understood; it will only become bearable once it is far past. Then she comes back, tells her husband only that it has been barely three years, borrows a hope she herself cannot name, agrees to work, feeds the child, and the storm is heard again. An English version that turns this into uplift ('she knew they would get through it'), into a feminist awakening, or into despair has rewritten the story. Its force is that she is genuinely comforted by something that leaves every material fact untouched.
crux.why: Everything structural serves this displacement. The supper begins in noise — storm outside, the baby banging a spoon, both parents laughing so absorbedly that they no longer hear the weather (p8). The silence begins privately, inside one mouthful of food, while the meal continues around her (p10–p13). The vision (p16–p17) is not marked off as dream, heaven, old age, or death, and the three figures are never identified as this family grown old, though the reader will want to make them so. On her return nothing is confessed: the long exchange with her husband (p21–p35) circles the same fact — only three years, and yet so much hardship — and ends in the most ordinary resolutions: work, clear up, sleep, rise early. The final line returns to the opening storm, now noticed in quiet, with the child asleep at the breast (p37–p38). The frame says: the evening is unchanged; only her distance from it has moved.

open_questions.question: The child is introduced in p2 unmistakably as a girl (女の子), yet both parents address her throughout as 坊や (p8, p30), ordinarily 'little boy' but used loosely for a baby. Keep 'Bōya' untranslated, normalise to a girl's name/endearment, or use a neutral English 'baby'? Each changes how much period/casual usage the English reader is asked to absorb, and silently 'correcting' it would falsify the text.
open_questions.why_it_matters: How the family is imagined in English from the first page.

open_questions.question: Are the three figures in the vision this family in extreme old age / after death, humanity in general, or an image the mother herself does not identify? The text gives 'three people' in dim light and says life will pass and come before 'an eternal night-like rest' (p17), but names nobody and sets no scene. A translation must not caption it ('she saw themselves grown old', 'she saw heaven'); the open question is only how much of the echo of the three at the table to let rhythm and pronoun choice suggest without stating it.
open_questions.why_it_matters: This is the interpretive fork the whole story hangs on; over-specifying it settles the crux by force.

open_questions.question: In p27 she feels she must tell him of 'something large, though she does not understand it herself' — is that unnamed hope the vision itself, which she then deliberately does not describe? She says only that three years have not yet passed. Keep the hope explicitly unnamed and untethered in English, resisting any phrasing ('her vision', 'what she had seen') that tells the reader she is referring to it.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Whether her reticence reads as failed communication or as the story's chosen form of intimacy.

body.reading:
The register is Taishō literary narration in historical kana, lyrical but not ornate, and it moves between two kinds of sentence that the English must keep distinct. Around the table the prose is crowded, physical and repetitive: the fat baby clutching the table, banging spoon and plate, the parents laughing, clearing bowls and the aluminium pot out of reach, feeding her and bolting their own rice in the gaps (p5–p10). From p10 the sentences lengthen and loosen, tense and viewpoint melt into the mother's interior, and by p16–p20 the prose is deliberately incantatory, saying the same things — long, endless, quiet, smiling, nostalgia and forgiveness, peace — until duration itself is felt. Keep that network of repeated words as repetition: 微笑 (smile), 疲れ (weariness), 静か (quiet), 遠い (far away), 夢のやう (like a dream), and above all 懐しみと許し (nostalgia/longing and forgiveness) and 安らかさ (peace, restfulness). Varying these for elegance, Berman's destruction of the underlying network of signification, would dissolve the vision's spell and with it the story. The same applies to 'long': the story, the suffering, and the life are all ながい, and the English should let that single dull word recur rather than find synonyms.

Keep the fatigue double from the start. In p3 both faces are unwrinkled and young, yet his eyes and her hair and shoulders already carry a deep, drowsy tiredness; p4 says the day's sorrows are about to flow away into the night's rest — and the whole story then tests that easy sentence. She is 'really still young' (p18) and feels completely old (p13) in the same evening; only three years have passed (p14, p22, p27) and they feel endless (p13). The English must hold both clocks without reconciling them, and must not let the narration age her voice into wisdom. Her husband is not a foil: he notices her silence twice (p19, p21) without understanding it, answers the one sentence she offers, and his encouragement (p28) — two years already gone, the baby will soon walk — is the practical, forward-looking version of her backward-looking vision. Neither is corrected by the narrator.

Likely fluent errors, beyond systematising the vision: giving the potato a cause ('undercooked', 'half-raw') where the text gives only sensation — hard as if frozen, gritty, extremely unpleasant, flavourless and cold (p11–p12), a tastelessness pointedly 'unconnected' to her that hands her a 'quiet, lonely, far-off heart'; that flatness is the trigger and must stay flat, not become a symbol glossed for the reader. Making the parents' laughter at the opening merely happy, where the text keeps calling it overflowing, helpless, forgetful (p8–p9) — it is exhaustion laughing. Turning the dialogue of p21–p35 into a marital heart-to-heart with beats of realisation; the lines are short, repeated, almost empty ('Really.' 'That's right.'), and their emptiness is the intimacy available. Softening the ending into cosiness: she bares a nipple and nurses the child (p35), he clears the table, and 'It's a storm' is whispered standing still (p38) — plain, bodily, and quiet, not a tableau of family warmth. And do not explain period or domestic terms in the prose; the beef, onion, carrot and potato in the dark-blue pot (p10) is the family's one substantial dish and needs no name imported for it.

Deliberate ambiguities to preserve: who is thinking p17 (the sentence widens from her mind toward a general truth and returns to her sigh in p18 — keep the seam unfused); whether the peace she imagines is old age, death, or simply distance in time; what the 'something large' is that she wants to tell him in p27; and the child's sex against her name, on which see the open questions. The story opens and closes on the storm (p1, p38) and twice notes the parents ceasing, then finally managing, to hear it (p8, p19): that hearing is the story's barometer of absorption and return, so keep both storm sentences bare and alike.
body.say: The story stands or falls on the mother's vision and on what is not done with it. One mouthful of badly cooked potato-mouthed, hard, gritty, tasteless-detaches her from the supper. Three years of married poverty suddenly feel like a whole lifetime already lived, she thinks she has grown completely old, and she sees three still figures endlessly telling the story of all human good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, trouble and joy, smiling and unmoving in nostalgia, forgiveness and deep peace(p16). The thought that follows is the story's core: life will pass, and only on the day after it has passed, in front of an eternal night-like rest, does everything become nostalgia and forgiveness(p17). Consolation here is entirely retrospective, almost posthumous. The present is not redeemed, improved, or even explained; it will only become lovable once it is far past. An English version that turns this into uplift (she learns hope), protest (she wakes to oppression), or despair has rewritten it. She keeps the vision to herself, tells her husband only that it has been barely three years, they agree to work, clear the table, rise early, and the storm p1 closes over p38 exactly unchanged.

items.english: Outside the door, dark now without anyone noticing, came the sound of fierce rain and wind. It was a {t:storm}.

The family had gathered at the {t:table} under the dim {t:lamp} hanging by the wall of the narrow room, about to have their evening meal. The father and mother were both still really young. And the child was a fat little girl, round all over, just able to stand by holding on to the {t:table}.

Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle on their faces. But in the man's sunken, gentle-looking eyes, in the shadow of his thick eyebrows, there was a colour of listless weariness. And in the woman's dark hair, and around her slender shoulders, there was a deeper weariness still, as if sunk down, and a peace like dozing.
notes: Kept 'weariness' and 'peace' here so the words can recur in the same form later, as in the Japanese.

items.english: The day was over. That day's sorrow and suffering were about to flow away into the peace of the night. And they, smiling and saying nothing, kept their eyes on everything the child did.

The child, standing unsteadily, was trying with both her hands — fat and round and short like a ball — without a moment's pause, and far too quickly, to stir about everything on the {t:table}. So, still smiling, they put all the {t:vessels} under the {t:table}. On the {t:table} only the child's {t:spoon-plate} was left.
But the child let out a noisy little cry, full of joy, and banged the {t:spoon-plate} down on the {t:table}.
notes: Kept 'smile/smiling' as the single word for the laughter-words in p4-p5, to hold the repetition the reading asks for.

revision.english: Outside the door, grown dark at some point, was the sound of hard rain and wind. A storm.

The parents and the child had gathered around the table under the dim electric light hung close to the wall of the narrow room, about to have their supper. Father and mother were both still really young. And the child was a round, plump little girl, just able to stand holding on to the table.

Neither the man nor the woman had a wrinkle yet in the face. But in the man's hollowed, kind-looking eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was a look of listless weariness. And in the color of the woman's dark hair and about her slender shoulders there was a still deeper, sunken weariness, and a drowsy peace.
The day had ended. The sorrow and suffering of that day were about to flow away into the peace of the night. And they, smiling in silence, kept all their eyes upon the child.

Standing unsteadily, the child kept trying, with fat, round hands short as balls, to sweep at the things on the table, without a moment's pause and far too fast. So, smiling, they put all the tea bowls and the teapot and the aluminum pot and the rest under the table. Left on the table were only the small spoon the child held and a single small plate.
But the child, giving a noisy little cry full of joy, banged the spoon and the plate down on the table.

"You won't do as you're told, will you." The young father stared at the small round arms and at the child's eyes with their long dark lashes, moving quick and bright without a pause, as if wondering what to do, and then, a smile spreading over his whole face, lightly pinching the child's round jutting cheek with his finger, he groped under the table for a large tea bowl and put it into the child's hands.
notes: I take 彼女の手 as the child's hands, receiving the bowl, not the mother's; the pronoun is shared in this text and the sentence context points to the child.

revision.english: She dished out rice for him, hot and fresh from the pot with the white steam rising thick, and handed it to him. Her young large eyes too, filled with a mother's joy, gazed at the child, not still for a moment, lovely like a small bird. And as if she could bear it no longer, murmuring under her breath, whatever can be the matter with this child, looking for all the world as if she found her too dear to know what to do, she called out firmly, "*Bōya*," but the smile overflowed her face and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And the three, as if they had forgotten everything, laughed together as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child, they set to their meal with warm bustle and with laughter and joy overflowing on its own. And in the rattling clatter they did not hear the sound of the rain and wind.
notes: I keep 坊や as *Bōya* rather than normalising to baby, to preserve the textual clash of a girl so addressed; see open question.
The murmur about the child is under-the-breath self-talk distinct from the spoken "*Bōya*."

revision.english: The young father kept his big red hand spread busily over the table. His eyes holding back the smile that welled up helplessly because of the child, he steadied the child and put a little food into her small red mouth. In the gaps, hastily opening his own wide mouth, he stuffed rice into it.

The mother, silent with bowed head by the wall, was serving onto a white plate the beef and onion, carrot and potato simmered in the deep blue pot. About to say something, she put a piece of potato, simmered sweet and soft, into her mouth and looked toward the man's face, but as if she had noticed something, she shut her mouth and stared vacantly at a place far away.

The potato in her mouth was hard as if frozen, and gritty, and tasted very bad. As if taken by surprise, she chewed it over silently with her front teeth, but her heart had already bowed down in loneliness.
notes: ざくざく kept as flat 'gritty': sensation only, without giving a cooking cause.

revision.english: She remembered the suffering and sorrow and weariness of her days. And the tasteless, unconnected, cold bad taste of the potato gave her a quiet, lonely, far off heart. She pictured the poor, sorrow filled, real life since her marriage.
notes: かゝはりのない rendered as 'unconnected' in the deliberate flat sense: the bad taste has nothing to do with her.

revision.english: And it seemed like a life that had gone on far too long. It suddenly seemed to her that she had grown quite old. And with a far off heart she quietly remembered the quiet days filled with tears, and the days spent threatened and afraid over material things, and each day of sorrow and suffering through sickness. payload.say: The story stands or falls on the mother's vision and on what is not done with it. One mouthful of badly cooked potato-mouthed, hard, gritty, tasteless-detaches her from the supper. Three years of married poverty suddenly feel like a whole lifetime already lived, she thinks she has grown completely old, and she sees three still figures endlessly telling the story of all human good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, trouble and joy, smiling and unmoving in nostalgia, forgiveness and deep peace(p16). The thought that follows is the story's core: life will pass, and only on the day after it has passed, in front of an eternal night-like rest, does everything become nostalgia and forgiveness(p17). Consolation here is entirely retrospective, almost posthumous. The present is not redeemed, improved, or even explained; it will only become lovable once it is far past. An English version that turns this into uplift (she learns hope), protest (she wakes to oppression), or despair has rewritten it. She keeps the vision to herself, tells her husband only that it has been barely three years, they agree to work, clear the table, rise early, and the storm p1 closes over p38 exactly unchanged.

crux.for_the_english: So: do not make the vision an explanation, a heaven, or a decision. Keep it still, repetitive, and unresolved, and let the return to work, breastfeeding, clearing up, and tomorrow be as plain as it is. Do not add psychology — 'she realised', 'she consoled herself', 'she resolved' — that the narration withholds, and do not warm the husband into obtuseness or tenderness to give the scene an antagonist or a rescuer.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on the mother's vision and on what is *not* done with it. A badly cooked potato — hard, gritty, tasteless in her mouth — does not prompt complaint, memory in the ordinary sense, or rebellion. It detaches her. Three years of married poverty suddenly feel like a whole lifetime already lived, she feels already old, and she sees, as in a dim picture, three quiet figures with heads together endlessly telling one another a story that contains all good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, trouble and joy, while nobody moves and everybody smiles, wrapped in nostalgia and forgiveness and a deep peace. The thought that follows is the crux: life passes, and only on the day after it has passed does everything turn to nostalgia and forgiveness, before an eternal, night-like rest. Consolation here is entirely retrospective and posthumous in feeling — the present is not redeemed, improved, or even understood; it will only become bearable once it is far past. Then she comes back, tells her husband only that it has been barely three years, borrows a hope she herself cannot name, agrees to work, feeds the child, and the storm is heard again. An English version that turns this into uplift ('she knew they would get through it'), into a feminist awakening, or into despair has rewritten the story. Its force is that she is genuinely comforted by something that leaves every material fact untouched.
crux.why: Everything structural serves this displacement. The supper begins in noise — storm outside, the baby banging a spoon, both parents laughing so absorbedly that they no longer hear the weather (p8). The silence begins privately, inside one mouthful of food, while the meal continues around her (p10–p13). The vision (p16–p17) is not marked off as dream, heaven, old age, or death, and the three figures are never identified as this family grown old, though the reader will want to make them so. On her return nothing is confessed: the long exchange with her husband (p21–p35) circles the same fact — only three years, and yet so much hardship — and ends in the most ordinary resolutions: work, clear up, sleep, rise early. The final line returns to the opening storm, now noticed in quiet, with the child asleep at the breast (p37–p38). The frame says: the evening is unchanged; only her distance from it has moved.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the slide unmarked and the vision unresolved: do not name it heaven, death, old age, or a flash-forward, do not convert its だらう / ようだ conjectures into certainty, and do not explain the potato as a symbol. Let the same repeated words — quiet, rest/peace, nostalgia/dearness, forgiveness, far, dream — accumulate in long, looping sentences rather than varying or compressing them for elegance.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on the mother's unmarked drift from the bad potato into a distant, end-of-life perspective in which the whole of life is already past and transfigured into nostalgia and forgiveness — while it remains undecidable whether that picture is death, extreme old age, or pure reverie.
crux.why: The turn is triggered by nothing grander than a grittily cold, tasteless potato (p11–p12), then the narration slips without signal from supper into p16's dim tableau of three motionless figures telling an endless story containing all good, evil, sorrow and joy, and p17's assertion that only on the day life has passed will everything change into 懐しみと許し. The shock of the piece is that this total retrospect is applied to a marriage of barely three years (p13–p14): she feels wholly aged, yet objectively almost nothing has elapsed.

crux.for_the_english: Preserve the durational loop and the circular weather: keep the repetitions and tense drift of the reverie, keep the short domestic exchanges flat and unadorned against it, and let the final 『嵐だな』 land as a return of the opening line rather than new information. Do not tidy the chronology (already three years / only three years / two years past) into a consistent summary.
crux.point: Time is experienced in two incompatible registers at once — one noisy evening and three exhausting years that feel like a lifetime, consoled only by projecting the redemptive 'that day' into an indefinite future and then immediately re-entering work and tomorrow.
crux.why: The storm opens the story (p1), is forgotten in the child's racket (p8), is first heard again inside the reverie itself (p19), and returns as the closing whisper (p38). Between those brackets the dialogue keeps recalculating the same span — 'only three years', 'already two years gone', 'a little longer' (p22–p35) — and the consolation of p20 resolves into nothing more visionary than nursing the child, clearing the table, and rising early tomorrow (p35–p36).

The parents and the child had gathered around the table under the dim electric light hung close to the wall of the narrow room, about to have their supper. Father and mother were both still really young. And the child was a round, plump little girl, just able to stand holding on to the table.

Neither the man nor the woman had a wrinkle yet in the face. But in the man's hollowed, kind-looking eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was a look of listless weariness. So, smiling, they put all the tea bowls and the teapot and the aluminum pot and the rest under the table. Left on the table were only the small spoon the child held and a single small plate.

Exchange is short, repeated, almost empty: どうして黙ってるの / なぜ黙ってるの, さうだなァ, 本当にね, まだ三年しか経たないんですものね. Husband plain-masculine 俺たち…なァ; wife polite のね/ませうね. Do not turn into heart-to-heart with beats of realisation, do not warm husband into obtuseness or tenderness, do not add psychology (she resolved/consoled herself). Emptiness is the intimacy.

小さな乳首をだして乳をのませ初めた; child with cheek to breast, eyes closed; clearing up, early rising tomorrow; whispered standing-still 嵐だな answering opening 嵐だ. Must stay plain, bodily, quiet — not cosy family tableau, not symbolic closure. Keep both storm sentences bare and alike.

motifs.english: Keep one small family: smile / smile / laughing. Do not vary to grin, chuckle, beam. Opening laughter is overflowing, helpless, forgetful exhaustion; vision smiling is motionless. Same word, changed state.
motifs.why: Network binds parents' helpless laughter at table to the still smiling of the vision figures. Varying it for elegance would dissolve the spell and hide that the same act has stilled.

motifs.english: Keep weariness / tiredness throughout; drowsy, sunken, deep. Do not upgrade to exhaustion-as-theme or downgrade to sleepiness.
source_forms: 打沈んだやうな深い疲れ
motifs.why: Establishes the fatigue double: faces still unwrinkled and young yet already carrying deep tiredness. The whole story tests p4's promise that night's rest will wash the day away.

motifs.english: Keep quiet / quietly / stillness as the same word. Do not vary to calm, gentle, silent for variety.
motifs.why: Moves from interior detachment (静かな淋しい遠くはなれた心) to vision stillness (物静か, 静かに安らかに) to returned house quiet (静まりかへった). One word tracks absorption and return.

motifs.english: Keep far / far-off / distant. Spatial word doing temporal work.
motifs.why: The mother's distance is rendered as space: staring far off, remembering with a far heart, seeing a far picture. Must recur, not be paraphrased as absent-minded or wistful.

motifs.english: Keep the exact paired phrase every time: nostalgia/longing and forgiveness. Do not alternate nostalgia/forgiveness with yearning/pardon, and do not shorten to one half.
source_forms: なつかしみと許しと安らかさ
motifs.why: The crux phrase. Everything will only on the day after passing turn into this pair. Identical repetition is the doctrine; synonyms rewrite it.

motifs.english: Keep peace / restfulness / rest. Same root for feeling and for night-like rest at end. Do not render as comfort, relief, serenity in rotation.
motifs.why: Tests p4: night's 安らかさ promised cheaply at start returns as deep peace of vision and as eternal night-like rest. Varying the English hides the test.

motifs.english: Keep long as long — dull, unvaried. Long story, long life, long suffering, endlessly continuing.
motifs.why: Deliberately monotonous duration-word. Finding synonyms (lengthy, protracted, eternal) would ennoble what the author keeps flat to make duration felt.

motifs.english: Keep like a dream and like a phantom picture as stated similes; do not harden into dream / hallucination nouns.
motifs.motif: like a dream, like a phantom
motifs.why: Marks the mother's defamiliarisation without marking it as dream, heaven or prophecy. Hardening it explains what text leaves open.

motifs.english: Keep storm and sound of rain-wind bare and alike in p1 and p38; keep the two not-hearings (p8) and hearings (p19). Barometer of absorption and return.
source_forms: 雨風の音を耳にしない
嵐の音を静かに耳にした
motifs.why: Frame: opens on storm, closes on storm. Forgetting it (laughter/noise) then hearing it again (quiet) measures her displacement. Must not be varied to tempest/gale or psychologised.

motifs.english: Keep three / three people / three years with numerals audible. Do not smooth away the echo, and do not state identity.
motifs.why: Three at table, three figures, barely three years — echo the reader will want to resolve into 'themselves grown old'. Keep the numbers identical so the echo sounds, without captioning it.

narration.english_tense: Past as default for narrative and interior report; keep gnomic present only where Japanese widens to general truth, chiefly p17 (life passes / everything turns…). Do not backshift vision into had-seen pluperfect explanation and do not present-tense the table bustle for vividness.
narration.frame: Single-evening interior, storm-enclosed: storm announced (p1) → crowded supper and laughter (p2–p9) → private detachment inside one mouthful (p10–p15) → vision and gloss (p16–p17) → sigh and return glance (p18) → noticed silence and unconfessed exchange about three years (p19–p35) → nursing, clearing, sleep, whispered storm (p36–p38). Evening unchanged; only her distance moved.
narration.narrator: Heterodiegetic third person, lyrical Taishō literary voice in historical kana; starts as even observer of the tableau, slides from p10 into mother's free-indirect interior without signals, widens toward aphorism in p17, then withdraws to plain exterior report. Never judges, never explains, never names.
narration.tense_habits: Historical-kana literary mix: past progressive ていた for tableau and ongoing action, stative ている / てゐる for states that persist into present, sudden present する for storm and gnomic statements, ところ・やうだ hedges for seeing-as. Viewpoint melts with tense from p10: longer looser sentences, subject-dropping, repetition replacing event.
timeline: One night only, during a storm: supper in a small room under a dark electric light
Married three years past (p14, p22, p25, p27); baby pre-walking, ~1 year; two years of hardship already gone, walking and work still ahead (p28, p34–p36)
Vision-time is unbounded: endless story, life after passing, eternal night-like rest (p16–p17) — no date, no place, deliberately unlocated

bible.say: A single-evening story that stands or falls on keeping the mother's vision still, repetitive and unexplained while the housework continues around it; hold every repeated word, both clocks (still young / already old, barely three years / endless), and the storm frame without warming, explaining or resolving them.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Minimal. No in-prose glosses for period food, aluminium pot, electric light, breastfeeding, or Bōya. Note only what sentence cannot give: e.g. one note on 坊や for a girl if Bōya is kept, one note on historical kana/ruby if edition policy needs it. Must pass the keikaku-means-plan test.
style_sheet.author_voice: Lyrical but not ornate; crowded, physical, repetitive at table (fat hands, banging, bolting rice), then lengthening and incantatory in vision. Keep paratactic plainness and deliberate dull repetition; resist ennoblement, clarification, and added psychology (she realised/resolved/consoled herself). Let ordinary resolutions — work, clear up, sleep, rise early — stay ordinary.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No personal names in text; keep role-terms in English lower case (young father, mother, baby) and never invent names. Keep 先生-style retention out — not applicable. For 坊や see keep_in_japanese: do not silently normalise to baby-boy or pet name without house decision and note.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: 坊や as Bōya (italicised, capital B) if house accepts untranslated address — because the clash girl-called-Bōya is textual data; otherwise neutral baby with a margin note recording the loss. No other Japanese retention needed; do not import dish-names. Macrons for romanisation where used (Bōya).
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 『』 for direct speech and ひとりごと思考独言; render in English double quotes with minimal tags, preserving unattributed turns and silences (p19, p21). Keep interior độc thoại (とふと口の中に独言…) distinct from spoken lines without adding 'she thought'.
style_sheet.register: Narrator: plain literary English, slightly period but not archaic; avoid modern colloquial bounce. Dialogue: husband plain rough-masculine, wife polite feminine-desu/masu; keep the gap audible without caricature or dialect.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Source ruby (卓《テーブル》, 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほほゑみ》, 茫然《ぼんやり》, 希《のぞみ》) is period reading-aid, not emphasis — do not carry into English as italics or parentheses. Use italics only for kept Japanese (Bōya) and, sparingly, for the babble うまうま if needed.

crux.for_the_english: So: do not make the vision an explanation, a heaven, or a decision. Keep it still, repetitive, and unresolved, and let the return to work, breastfeeding, clearing up, and tomorrow be as plain as it is. Do not add psychology — 'she realised', 'she consoled herself', 'she resolved' — that the narration withholds, and do not warm the husband into obtuseness or tenderness to give the scene an antagonist or a rescuer.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on the mother's vision and on what is *not* done with it. A badly cooked potato — hard, gritty, tasteless in her mouth — does not prompt complaint, memory in the ordinary sense, or rebellion. It detaches her. Three years of married poverty suddenly feel like a whole lifetime already lived, she feels already old, and she sees, as in a dim picture, three quiet figures with heads together endlessly telling one another a story that contains all good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, trouble and joy, while nobody moves and everybody smiles, wrapped in nostalgia and forgiveness and a deep peace. The thought that follows is the crux: life passes, and only on the day after it has passed does everything turn to nostalgia and forgiveness, before an eternal, night-like rest. Consolation here is entirely retrospective and posthumous in feeling — the present is not redeemed, improved, or even understood; it will only become bearable once it is far past. Then she comes back, tells her husband only that it has been barely three years, borrows a hope she herself cannot name, agrees to work, feeds the child, and the storm is heard again. An English version that turns this into uplift ('she knew they would get through it'), into a feminist awakening, or into despair has rewritten the story. Its force is that she is genuinely comforted by something that leaves every material fact untouched.
crux.why: Everything structural serves this displacement. The supper begins in noise — storm outside, the baby banging a spoon, both parents laughing so absorbedly that they no longer hear the weather (p8). The silence begins privately, inside one mouthful of food, while the meal continues around her (p10–p13). The vision (p16–p17) is not marked off as dream, heaven, old age, or death, and the three figures are never identified as this family grown old, though the reader will want to make them so. On her return nothing is confessed: the long exchange with her husband (p21–p35) circles the same fact — only three years, and yet so much hardship — and ends in the most ordinary resolutions: work, clear up, sleep, rise early. The final line returns to the opening storm, now noticed in quiet, with the child asleep at the breast (p37–p38). The frame says: the evening is unchanged; only her distance from it has moved.

open_questions.question: The child is introduced in p2 unmistakably as a girl (女の子), yet both parents address her throughout as 坊や (p8, p30), ordinarily 'little boy' but used loosely for a baby. Keep 'Bōya' untranslated, normalise to a girl's name/endearment, or use a neutral English 'baby'? Each changes how much period/casual usage the English reader is asked to absorb, and silently 'correcting' it would falsify the text.
open_questions.why_it_matters: How the family is imagined in English from the first page.

open_questions.question: Are the three figures in the vision this family in extreme old age / after death, humanity in general, or an image the mother herself does not identify? The text gives 'three people' in dim light and says life will pass and come before 'an eternal night-like rest' (p17), but names nobody and sets no scene. A translation must not caption it ('she saw themselves grown old', 'she saw heaven'); the open question is only how much of the echo of the three at the table to let rhythm and pronoun choice suggest without stating it.
open_questions.why_it_matters: This is the interpretive fork the whole story hangs on; over-specifying it settles the crux by force.

open_questions.question: In p27 she feels she must tell him of 'something large, though she does not understand it herself' — is that unnamed hope the vision itself, which she then deliberately does not describe? She says only that three years have not yet passed. Keep the hope explicitly unnamed and untethered in English, resisting any phrasing ('her vision', 'what she had seen') that tells the reader she is referring to it.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Whether her reticence reads as failed communication or as the story's chosen form of intimacy.

reading.reading:
The register is Taishō literary narration in historical kana, lyrical but not ornate, and it moves between two kinds of sentence that the English must keep distinct. Around the table the prose is crowded, physical and repetitive: the fat baby clutching the table, banging spoon and plate, the parents laughing, clearing bowls and the aluminium pot out of reach, feeding her and bolting their own rice in the gaps (p5–p10). From p10 the sentences lengthen and loosen, tense and viewpoint melt into the mother's interior, and by p16–p20 the prose is deliberately incantatory, saying the same things — long, endless, quiet, smiling, nostalgia and forgiveness, peace — until duration itself is felt. Keep that network of repeated words as repetition: 微笑 (smile), 疲れ (weariness), 静か (quiet), 遠い (far away), 夢のやう (like a dream), and above all 懐しみと許し (nostalgia/longing and forgiveness) and 安らかさ (peace, restfulness). Varying these for elegance, Berman's destruction of the underlying network of signification, would dissolve the vision's spell and with it the story. The same applies to 'long': the story, the suffering, and the life are all ながい, and the English should let that single dull word recur rather than find synonyms.

Keep the fatigue double from the start. In p3 both faces are unwrinkled and young, yet his eyes and her hair and shoulders already carry a deep, drowsy tiredness; p4 says the day's sorrows are about to flow away into the night's rest — and the whole story then tests that easy sentence. She is 'really still young' (p18) and feels completely old (p13) in the same evening; only three years have passed (p14, p22, p27) and they feel endless (p13). The English must hold both clocks without reconciling them, and must not let the narration age her voice into wisdom. Her husband is not a foil: he notices her silence twice (p19, p21) without understanding it, answers the one sentence she offers, and his encouragement (p28) — two years already gone, the baby will soon walk — is the practical, forward-looking version of her backward-looking vision. Neither is corrected by the narrator.

Likely fluent errors, beyond systematising the vision: giving the potato a cause ('undercooked', 'half-raw') where the text gives only sensation — hard as if frozen, gritty, extremely unpleasant, flavourless and cold (p11–p12), a tastelessness pointedly 'unconnected' to her that hands her a 'quiet, lonely, far-off heart'; that flatness is the trigger and must stay flat, not become a symbol glossed for the reader. Making the parents' laughter at the opening merely happy, where the text keeps calling it overflowing, helpless, forgetful (p8–p9) — it is exhaustion laughing. Turning the dialogue of p21–p35 into a marital heart-to-heart with beats of realisation; the lines are short, repeated, almost empty ('Really.' 'That's right.'), and their emptiness is the intimacy available. Softening the ending into cosiness: she bares a nipple and nurses the child (p35), he clears the table, and 'It's a storm' is whispered standing still (p38) — plain, bodily, and quiet, not a tableau of family warmth. And do not explain period or domestic terms in the prose; the beef, onion, carrot and potato in the dark-blue pot (p10) is the family's one substantial dish and needs no name imported for it.

Deliberate ambiguities to preserve: who is thinking p17 (the sentence widens from her mind toward a general truth and returns to her sigh in p18 — keep the seam unfused); whether the peace she imagines is old age, death, or simply distance in time; what the 'something large' is that she wants to tell him in p27; and the child's sex against her name, on which see the open questions. The story opens and closes on the storm (p1, p38) and twice notes the parents ceasing, then finally managing, to hear it (p8, p19): that hearing is the story's barometer of absorption and return, so keep both storm sentences bare and alike.
reading.say: The story stands or falls on the mother's vision and on what is not done with it. One mouthful of badly cooked potato-mouthed, hard, gritty, tasteless-detaches her from the supper. Three years of married poverty suddenly feel like a whole lifetime already lived, she thinks she has grown completely old, and she sees three still figures endlessly telling the story of all human good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, trouble and joy, smiling and unmoving in nostalgia, forgiveness and deep peace(p16). The thought that follows is the story's core: life will pass, and only on the day after it has passed, in front of an eternal night-like rest, does everything become nostalgia and forgiveness(p17). Consolation here is entirely retrospective, almost posthumous. The present is not redeemed, improved, or even explained; it will only become lovable once it is far past. An English version that turns this into uplift (she learns hope), protest (she wakes to oppression), or despair has rewritten it. She keeps the vision to herself, tells her husband only that it has been barely three years, they agree to work, clear the table, rise early, and the storm p1 closes over p38 exactly unchanged.

voice_takes.label: spare and slightly cool
voice_takes.line: Clean modern literary English, short table sentences and long level sentences for the vision, repetition kept word-for-word, no period flavouring.

voice_takes.label: warmer and more lyrical
voice_takes.line: Softer cadence and fuller phrasing around the parents and child, letting the smiles and weariness glow a little, at the risk of sentimentality the text avoids.

voice_takes.label: plainer and more literal
voice_takes.line: Flatter diction, repetitions and slight awkwardnesses of the original left visible, the vision almost chant-like, trusting bareness over English grace.

casual.en: Outside the door, where it had grown dark at some point, was the sound of hard rain and wind. A storm.
casual.ja: いつか暗くなった戸の外に、激しい雨風の音がする、嵐だ。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The parents and the child had gathered around the table under the dim electric light hung close to the wall of the narrow room, about to have their supper. Father and mother were both still really young. And the child was a round, plump little girl, just able to stand holding on to the table.
casual.ja: 親子は、狭い部屋の壁際にぶらさがった、暗い電燈の下の卓に集まって、今夜食をしようとしてゐた。まだ本当に父も母も若かった。そして子供は漸く卓につかまって、立ってる事が出来る程の、くり〳〵と肥ってる女の子だった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Neither the man nor the woman had a wrinkle yet in the face. But in the man's hollowed, kind-looking eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was a look of listless weariness. And in the color of the woman's dark hair and about her slender shoulders there was a still deeper, sunken weariness, and a drowsy peace.
casual.ja: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The day had ended. The sorrow and suffering of that day were about to flow away into the peace of the night. And they, smiling in silence, kept their eyes fixed on the child, on all of her.
casual.ja: 一日が終ったのであった。その日の悲しみも苦しみも、夜の安らかさに流れやうとしてゐるのだった。そして、彼等は黙って微笑しながら、その子供のすべてに瞳を注いだ。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Standing unsteadily, the child kept trying, with fat round hands, short like balls, to sweep at the things on the table, without a moment's pause and far too fast. So, smiling, they put all the tea bowls and the teapot and the aluminum pot and the rest under the table. Left on the table were only the small spoon the child held and a single small plate.
casual.ja: 子供は、あぶなさうに立ちながら、肥えてまるく鞠のやうに短い両手で、すこしのすきまもなく、そしてあまりに早くテーブルの上のものを掻き廻さうとしてゐた。それで彼等は微笑みみながら、すべて茶碗や土瓶、アルミ鍋などを、テーブルの下に置いた。テーブルの上には、わづか子供の持つ小さなスプーンと小皿が一枚残されたばかりであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: But the child, giving a noisy little cry full of joy, banged the spoon and the plate down on the table.
casual.ja: けれども子供は、さわがしい、小さなよろこびに満ちた叫声を上げて、スプーンと皿をテーブルの上にたゝきつけた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "You won't do as you're told, will you." The young father stared at the small round arms and at the child's eyes with their long dark lashes, moving quick and bright without a pause, as if wondering what to do, and then, a smile spreading over his whole face, lightly pinching the child's round jutting cheek with his finger, he groped under the table for a large tea bowl and put it into the child's hands.
casual.ja: 『きかない奴だな。』若い父親は、その小さなまるい腕や、敏捷に怜悧にすきもなく動いてる、黒みがちの睫のながい子供の瞳をぢっと見てゐると、どうしたらいゝだらうといふやうに、やがて顔一ぱいな微笑を持って、子供のまるくつき出た頬を指で一寸つまみながら、大きな茶碗をテーブルの下から探すやうにしてとると、彼女の手に渡した。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The mother dished out rice for him, hot and fresh from the pot with the white steam rising thick, and handed it to him. Her young large eyes too, filled with a mother's joy, gazed at the child, not still for a moment, lovely like a small bird. And as if she could bear it no longer, murmuring under her breath, whatever can be the matter with this child, looking for all the world as if she found her too dear to know what to do, she called out firmly, "*Bōya*," but the smile overflowed across her face and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And the three, as if they had forgotten everything, laughed together as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child, they set to their meal with warm bustle and with laughter and joy overflowing on its own. And in the rattling clatter they did not hear the sound of the rain and wind.
casual.ja: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。
casual.label: house-checked

notes.body: Bōya is usually a fond way to call a little boy. Here it is used for a baby girl, a casual period use the translation keeps as is.

casual.en: The young father kept his big red hand spread busily over the table. Holding back the smile that welled up helplessly because of the child, he steadied the child and put a little food into her small red mouth. In between, hastily opening his own wide mouth, he shovelled rice into it.
casual.ja: 若い父親は、彼の赤く大きな片手を忙しくテーブルの上に拡げてゐた。そしてその眼は子供によって仕方がなく湧き出た笑を堪へながら、子供をさゝへて、その小さな赤い口に僅の食物を入れてやった。そのすきに彼は、あわたゞしく大きな口を開けた、彼は彼自身の口のなかに御飯を押し込んだ。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The mother, silent with bowed head by the wall, was serving onto a white plate the beef and onion, carrot and potato simmered in the deep blue pot. About to say something, she put a piece of potato, simmered sweet and soft, into her mouth and looked toward the man's face, but as if she had noticed something, she shut her mouth and stared vacantly at a place far away.
casual.ja: 母親は、壁によって黙ってうつむきながら藍色の深い鍋に煮た牛肉と玉葱と、人参とジャガ芋とを白い皿に盛ってゐた。そしてなにか云はうとして、甘く柔かく煮たジャガ芋を口のなかに入れて、男の顔を見たが、彼女はなにかに気がついたやうに、ふと口を閉ぢて茫然と遠い所を見た。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The potato in her mouth was hard as if frozen, and gritty, and tasted very bad. As if taken by surprise, she went on chewing silently with her front teeth, but her heart had already sunk in loneliness.
casual.ja: 彼女の口のなかのジャガ芋が、丁度凍ったかのやうに固くざく〳〵してゐて、非常に不味かったのだった。彼女はふと驚いたやうに黙って前歯でかみなほしたが、彼女の心は、いつか淋しくうつむいてしまってゐた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: She remembered the suffering and sorrow and weariness of her days. And the tasteless, unconnected, cold bad taste of the potato gave her a quiet, lonely, far off heart. She pictured the poor, sorrow filled, real life since her marriage.
casual.ja: 彼女は日々の苦しみや悲しみ疲れを思出したのであった。そしてジャガ芋の無味な、かゝはりのない冷やかな不味さが、彼女に静かな淋しい遠くはなれた心を与へた。彼女は結婚後の貧しい悲しみにみちた現実の生活を思ひ浮べたのであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: And it seemed like a life that had gone on far too long. It suddenly seemed to her that she had grown quite old. And her far-off heart quietly remembered the quiet days filled with tears, and the days spent threatened and afraid over material things, and each day of sorrow and suffering through sickness. But to her as she remembered now, everything was like a dream. Suffering and sorrow were like a nostalgic dream.
casual.ja: そして、それがあまりに永く引きつゞいた生活のやうにも思はれた。彼女はふと自分がすっかり老いてしまったかのやうに考へられた。そして静かに涙にみちた日のことや、物質の為めに脅かされ恐れてすごした日々や、病の為めに悲しみ苦しんだその日その日のことを遠い心が静かに思出してゐるのだった。けれどもいま思出してる彼女には、すべてが夢のやうであった。苦しみも悲しみもなつかしい夢のやうであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: And when she thought of it, it was only barely three years of life since marriage.
casual.ja: そして考へて見れば、わづかに結婚後の三年ばかりの生活にすぎない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Before she knew it, as if caught by something, she gazed vacantly far into the distance. Her quiet heart was already seeing a picture like a phantom.
casual.ja: 彼女は、いつとなく何物にか気をとられたやうに、ぼんやりと遠くの方を見てゐた。彼女のその静かな心が、いつか幻のやうな絵を見てゐたのであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: In a dim light, three people, quiet as that light, drew close with heads together, telling a long story. The story seemed to go on and on between them, too long and without end. And in that story seemed to be told all the good and evil of the world, sorrow and suffering and anger and trouble, joy, everything. But those who told it and those who listened to it only went on quietly and peacefully, still smiling, and did not move at all. With their heads bent and their eyes lowered, only a quiet nostalgia and forgiveness seemed to wrap them. And a deep, deep peace showed itself in all of them.
casual.ja: それは淡暗い光りのなかに、そしてその光りのやうに物静かな三人の人たちが、より合って頭をあつめてながい物語りをしてゐるのだった。その物語りは、あまりにながく絶えることなく彼等の間につゞけられてゐるやうであった。そしてその物語りのなかには、すべて世の中の善や悪や、かなしみや苦しみ怒りもなやみも、よろこびもすべてが語られてるやうだった。けれども話す人も聞く人も、たゞ静かに安らかにぢっと微笑をつゞけてゐるばかりであって、彼等は少しも動かなかった。首をかたむけて眼を伏せながら、そして、そこにはたゞ静かななつかしみと、許しとが彼等をつつんでゐるやうに見えた。そしてまたそこには深い〳〵安らかさが彼等のすべてに表はれてゐるのであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: All things in the world, a life, will pass. And only on the day after it has passed will everything, all things, turn to nostalgia and forgiveness. And then they will be forever before a night-like rest.
casual.ja: 世の中の總ての事、人生は過去るであらう。そして過去った其日に初めて總てが、總ての事が懐しみと許しとに変る事だらう。そして其時彼等は永久に夜の様な安息の前にあるのであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The far picture was reflected dark and quiet in the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes, far into the future, with a lonely peace, that picture could still be seen. Young as she was, alone she gave a lonely, secret sigh, and glancing at the littered table and at the faces of her husband and child, she said nothing.
casual.ja: 遠い絵が暗く静かに、彼女の眼の底に映ってゐた。また瞳の底を通して遠く未来に、淋しい安らかさを持って、その絵が見えるのであった。若い彼女は一人で淋しいひそかな溜息をついた、そして、とり散らされたテーブルの上と、夫と子供の顔をちらと見ながら黙ってゐた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Why are you so quiet?" the man said, looking at the woman's face as if puzzled. She hurried to say something, but unable to put anything into words she fell silent, and her gaze drifted far away again. And she saw the phantom-like picture again. Then for the first time she quietly heard the sound of the storm outside the door. She said nothing.
casual.ja: 『どうして黙ってるの。』男は、ふと不思議さうに女の顔を見て声をかけた。彼女は、あわてゝなにかを云はうとしたが、一口には何事も云ひかねて黙ってしまふと、再びその眼が遠く走ってしまった。そして彼女は、また幻の絵を見たのだった。彼女は、その時はじめて戸の外の嵐の音を、静かに耳にした。彼女はなにも云はずにゐた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Yes. That day is there. The day when everything turns to nostalgia and forgiveness, and peace. After a long life, and after long sorrow, and after long suffering, on the day after, there is that day of peaceful nostalgia and forgiveness. What are the suffering and sorrow of each single day. What are the weariness and trouble of each single day. Before she knew it she had a smile on her face.
casual.ja: さうだ。あの日があるのだ。あのすべてがなつかしみと許しと、安らかさに変る日があるのだった。ながい生活の後に、またながい悲しみの後に、またながい苦しみのその後の日に、あの安らかななつかしみと許しの日があるのだ。一日々々の苦しみや悲しみがなんだらう。一日々々の疲れやなやみがなんだらう。彼女はいつとなしに微笑を浮べてゐた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Why are you so quiet?" the man said again. She raised her head as if startled, smiling as if with nostalgia, "Still, really only a very little time has passed since we married, hasn't it," she said, as if asking him too to remember, all sorts of things, even the happy things from before they married.
casual.ja: 『なぜ黙ってるの。』男は再び声をかけた。彼女は驚いたやうに頭を上げて、なつかしさうに笑ひながら、
casual.label: house-checked

casual.ja: 『まだ本当にわづかしか経ちませんのね、結婚してから。』
casual.label: house-checked

casual.ja: と男にも思出して、種々のことを、結婚前の楽しかったことまでも、思出して下さいと云ふやうに云った。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "That's right," the man too looked up and said. "It comes to only three years. But we have suffered in all sorts of ways, haven't we."
casual.ja: 『さうだなァ。』男も眼を上げて云った。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.ja: 『たった三年にしかならないんだな。けれども、俺たちはいろ〳〵苦労したなァ。』
casual.label: house-checked

casual.ja: 『本当にね。』彼女は、また眼を伏せてあの絵を見ようとした。が、すぐに、
casual.label: house-checked

casual.label: house-checked

casual.ja: 『さうだ、一日々々いろ〳〵なことに疲らされなやまされ苦しまされても、二年はもう過ぎたんだからな。もうしばらくすると、坊やも歩るくやうになるんだから。』
casual.label: house-checked

casual.ja: 男は、手持ぶさたのやうにスプーンを持って立ってる子供を見た。彼女は、すぐに嬉しさうに、
casual.label: house-checked

casual.label: house-checked

casual.ja: 『うま〳〵〳〵〳〵。』とスプーンをテーブルにたゝきつけた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The father hurriedly put rice into the child's mouth.
casual.ja: 父親は、あわてゝ子供の口に御飯を入れてやった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: After a while they laid down their chopsticks.
casual.ja: 彼等は、やがて箸をおいた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Only a little while longer." The man said firmly, as if to himself.
casual.ja: 『もう少しの間だ。』男は強く独言のやうに云った。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Yes, let's work, shall we." She said calmly, peacefully. Then, holding the child on her lap, she bared a small nipple and began to nurse.
casual.ja: 『さうね、私たちは働きませうね。』彼女は、おちついて安らかに云った。そして子供を膝の上に抱きながら、小さな乳首をだして乳をのませ初めた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Come, let's clear away. And sleep. Let's get up early tomorrow."
casual.ja: 『さ、あとを片づけよう。そして寝よう、明日は早く起きようぢゃないか。』
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: After a while the man stood up. When he was about to begin clearing the table, the child had already closed her eyes with her cheek against the breast. All around had grown quiet.
casual.ja: やがて、男は立ち上った。そしてテーブルを片づけ初めようとした時、もはや子供は乳房に頬をつけて眼を閉ぢてゐた。あたりは静まりかへった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "A storm." The man whispered, standing still.
casual.ja: 『嵐だな。』男は、立ちどまってさゝやいた。
casual.label: house-checked

curious.en: Outside the door, where it had grown dark at some point, was the sound of hard rain and wind. A storm.
curious.ja: いつか暗くなった戸の外に、激しい雨風の音がする、嵐だ。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The parents and the child had gathered around the table under the dim electric light hung close to the wall of the narrow room, about to have their supper. curious.ja: 親子は、狭い部屋の壁際にぶらさがった、暗い電燈の下の卓に集まって、今夜食をしようとしてゐた。まだ本当に父も母も若かった。そして子供は漸く卓につかまって、立ってる事が出来る程の、くり〳〵と肥ってる女の子だった。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Neither the man nor the woman had a wrinkle yet in the face. But in the man's hollowed, kind-looking eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was a look of listless weariness. And in the color of the woman's dark hair and about her slender shoulders there was a still deeper, sunken weariness, and a drowsy peace.
curious.ja: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The day had ended. The sorrow and suffering of that day were about to flow away into the peace of the night. And they, smiling in silence, kept their eyes fixed on the child, on all of her.
curious.ja: 一日が終ったのであった。その日の悲しみも苦しみも、夜の安らかさに流れやうとしてゐるのだった。そして、彼等は黙って微笑しながら、その子供のすべてに瞳を注いだ。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Standing unsteadily, the child kept trying, with fat round hands, short like balls, to sweep at the things on the table, without a moment's pause and far too fast. curious.ja: 子供は、あぶなさうに立ちながら、肥えてまるく鞠のやうに短い両手で、すこしのすきまもなく、そしてあまりに早くテーブルの上のものを掻き廻さうとしてゐた。それで彼等は微笑みみながら、すべて茶碗や土瓶、アルミ鍋などを、テーブルの下に置いた。テーブルの上には、わづか子供の持つ小さなスプーンと小皿が一枚残されたばかりであった。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: But the child, giving a noisy little cry full of joy, banged the spoon and the plate down on the table.
curious.ja: けれども子供は、さわがしい、小さなよろこびに満ちた叫声を上げて、スプーンと皿をテーブルの上にたゝきつけた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "You won't do as you're told, will you." curious.ja: 『きかない奴だな。』若い父親は、その小さなまるい腕や、敏捷に怜悧にすきもなく動いてる、黒みがちの睫のながい子供の瞳をぢっと見てゐると、どうしたらいゝだらうといふやうに、やがて顔一ぱいな微笑を持って、子供のまるくつき出た頬を指で一寸つまみながら、大きな茶碗をテーブルの下から探すやうにしてとると、彼女の手に渡した。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The mother dished out rice for him, hot and fresh from the pot with the white steam rising thick, and handed it to him. notes.body: Bōya is usually a fond way to call a little boy. Here it is used for a baby girl, a casual period use the translation keeps as is.
